how-to-fix-spf-too-many-dns-lookups.html.text:
← Back to Email Authentication Checker

SPF PermError: fixing “too many DNS lookups”

An SPF record is allowed 10 DNS lookups. Go over, and RFC 7208 §4.6.4 says the receiver must return PermError — for every message you send, permanently, until the record is shortened. Nothing warns you. There is no bounce that says “your SPF record is too long”.

This is the most common real-world SPF bug, and it has a boring cause: you add one include: for your mail host, another for your invoicing tool, another for your helpdesk, another for the newsletter — and one day the total quietly crosses 10.

What actually breaks (and why you might not notice)

SPF evaluation stops at the limit and returns PermError. Receivers read that as “this domain’s SPF cannot be evaluated”, so the SPF half of DMARC alignment fails. If your DKIM signature is present and aligned, DMARC can still pass on DKIM alone — which is exactly why a domain over the limit often keeps delivering and the bug survives for months. You lose the redundancy silently, and find out on the day DKIM breaks or a receiver weighs SPF on its own.

Which mechanisms cost a lookup

TermCosts a lookup?Notes
include:Yes — 1Plus everything inside the record it pulls in
redirect=Yes — 1Plus everything inside the record it points at
a / a:Yes — 1One per mechanism
mx / mx:Yes — 1Capped separately at 10 MX records returned
exists:Yes — 1One per mechanism
ptrYes — 1§5.5 says do not publish it — see below
ip4: / ip6:NoAddress literals; no DNS query needed
allNoMatches without a query
exp=NoFetched only when a message fails, outside the budget

The budget is cumulative across the whole chain. A lookup inside a record you include: spends from the same 10 as one in your own record. This is what makes the bug hard to see by eye: a record with four include: terms looks like four lookups and can easily be eighteen.

The 10 are beyond the initial TXT query that fetches your record, so reading your own SPF does not spend from the budget.

Count yours

The Email Authentication Checker walks every include: and redirect= recursively and reports the chain total against the limit, naming the exact record each lookup came from. In the browser, or from a terminal:

npx --yes github:Duncan-Haywood/monorepo-projects#main \
  --package-lock=false ventures/email-auth-check/cli.mjs example.com

Or clone the repository and run node ventures/email-auth-check/cli.mjs example.com. Both query public DNS-over-HTTPS directly from wherever you run them; nothing is sent to us.

Six ways back under the limit

1. Delete includes for tools you no longer send from

The cheapest fix and usually the largest. Every SaaS trial that once asked you to add an include: is still costing you a lookup. Go through the list and ask, per entry, “does mail still leave from this?”

2. Replace a and mx with the addresses they resolve to

If your mail server has a stable, static IP, ip4:203.0.113.10 does the same job as mx for zero lookups. This is safe precisely where flattening an ESP is not: it is your address, and you control when it changes.

3. Remove ptr

RFC 7208 §5.5 says ptr SHOULD NOT be published and that receivers may ignore it. It spends a lookup, it is slow, and its answer is not dependable. Deleting it is nearly always free.

4. Move bulk mail to a subdomain

Send newsletters from news.example.com and transactional mail from mail.example.com. Each subdomain gets its own 10-lookup budget and its own SPF record, so the ESP includes move off the parent domain entirely. This is the fix that keeps working as you add tools, rather than buying you two or three more.

5. Consolidate overlapping vendors

Two tools that both send “your receipt” email are two includes. Sometimes the honest fix is fewer tools.

6. Flatten — knowing what it costs

Flattening replaces an include: with the ip4:/ip6: ranges it resolves to today. It genuinely removes lookups. It also freezes your provider’s IP list at the moment you flattened it: when they add or move a range, your record still authorizes the old one, and mail starts failing SPF with no error anywhere to explain it. That is strictly worse than the problem you started with, because PermError is at least visible.

Flatten only if something re-flattens on a schedule and alerts you when the upstream record changes. If that is not in place, prefer fix 4.

A worked example

v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net include:servers.mcsv.net mx a ~all

Four visible lookup terms plus mx and a — six, by eye. Walk into them and _spf.google.com alone contributes several through its own nested includes. Chains shaped like this routinely total 12–18. The fix here is usually (4): give the marketing tool its own subdomain, leaving the parent record with the mail host and a couple of ip4: literals.

After you change the record

  • Wait for the old record’s TTL to expire before judging the result.
  • Re-run the check and confirm the chain total, not just your own record’s term count.
  • Publish exactly one SPF TXT record. Two is its own PermError, independent of the lookup count.
  • If you moved sending to a subdomain, give that subdomain its own SPF record — it does not inherit the parent’s.

Common questions

What does an SPF PermError from too many DNS lookups actually break?

SPF evaluation stops and returns PermError for every message from the domain, not just some of them. Receivers treat PermError as "this domain's SPF cannot be evaluated", so the SPF half of DMARC alignment fails. If DKIM is signing and aligned, DMARC can still pass on DKIM alone — which is why a domain over the limit often keeps delivering and the bug goes unnoticed for months.

Which SPF mechanisms count toward the 10-lookup limit?

RFC 7208 section 4.6.4 counts the include, a, mx, ptr and exists mechanisms, plus the redirect modifier. Each one costs exactly one lookup toward the budget. The ip4, ip6 and all mechanisms cost nothing because they need no DNS query, and the exp modifier is only fetched when a message fails, so it is outside the budget too.

Is the limit 10 lookups or 11?

The budget is 10 lookups beyond the initial TXT query that fetches the record itself, so fetching your own SPF record does not spend from the 10. The count is also cumulative across the whole chain: a lookup inside a record you include: spends from the same budget as one in your own record.

Does SPF flattening fix it permanently?

No. Flattening replaces an include: with the ip4/ip6 ranges it resolves to today, which does remove lookups — but it also freezes your sending provider's IP list at the moment you flattened it. When that provider adds or moves a range, your record still authorizes the old one and your mail starts failing SPF with no error anywhere to explain it. Flattening trades a visible failure now for a silent one later unless something re-flattens it on a schedule.

Should I use the ptr mechanism in SPF?

No. RFC 7208 section 5.5 says ptr SHOULD NOT be published, and that receivers may ignore it entirely. It costs a lookup from your budget, it is slow, and its result is not dependable. If a record you inherited contains ptr, removing it is almost always both safe and a free lookup back.

Why does my SPF record pass in one checker and fail in another?

Most commonly because the other checker counted only the mechanisms in your own record rather than walking into each include: and counting what is inside it. The limit applies to the whole recursive chain, so a record with four include: terms can be well over 10 while looking like four. A checker that reports a per-record count rather than a chain total will disagree with what a receiver computes.

Email Authentication Checker

Type a domain that sends its own email (transactional or marketing) and this looks up its SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and BIMI DNS records over public DNS-over-HTTPS and reports what each one says and why it matters -- too many SPF DNS-lookup mechanisms (the single most common real-world SPF bug), a +all catch-all that authorizes anyone to send as your domain, a missing or monitor-only DMARC policy that leaves you spoofable while looking configured, and revoked or missing DKIM keys. Every finding names the exact record it read. This is evidence about your DNS, not a verdict -- never "your domain is secure", always "here is what your records say and what that means."

Check a domain

Runs directly from your browser to Cloudflare's public DNS resolver. Nothing is uploaded to this site.

Report:

Prefer the command line, or want to gate CI on it?

The Node CLI runs the identical checks with no dependencies to install, and its exit code (0 = no danger-severity finding and every lookup completed; 1 otherwise) is usable as a regression gate for your own domain's mail configuration:

node cli.mjs yourdomain.com
node cli.mjs yourdomain.com --json

Get cli.mjs, lookup.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo -- plain Node, nothing to install. It queries the same public DNS resolver as this page, straight from your own machine; nothing goes through this site either way.

Common questions

Why is my email going to spam?

The most common technical causes are a missing or misconfigured SPF record, no DKIM signing, or a missing/monitor-only (p=none) DMARC record -- mailbox providers use all three as spam and spoofing signals. This tool reads exactly what your domain's DNS currently says for each one and names what to fix. It cannot see reputation, content, or sending-volume factors, which also affect spam placement.

What does "too many SPF DNS lookups" mean, and why does it break everything?

RFC 7208 caps SPF evaluation at 10 DNS lookups (each include:, a, mx, ptr, exists mechanism and each redirect= modifier counts, and include: chains recursively). Go over 10 and the result is a permanent error (PermError) -- meaning SPF fails for every message from your domain, for every receiver, whether or not the message is legitimate. This is usually caused by stacking one include: per marketing or support tool over time until the total quietly crosses 10.

What is DMARC p=none and why is it a problem?

p=none means DMARC is in monitor-only mode: receivers are asked to take no action even on a message that fails alignment. It is the most common real-world gap, because a domain with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all present looks fully configured while still being completely spoofable. p=none is a reasonable first step while you review the aggregate reports it generates; moving to p=quarantine or p=reject is what actually stops spoofed mail.

Does a clean report mean my email is fully secure?

No. This reads SPF, DKIM, DMARC and BIMI DNS records and reports what they say -- it is evidence about your domain's mail-authentication configuration, not a determination that your email is secure or that mail will reach the inbox. Deliverability also depends on sender reputation, content, list hygiene, and each receiver's own policies, none of which live in DNS.

Why check nine DKIM selector names instead of just looking up DKIM directly?

DKIM keys are published at a selector-specific name (<selector>._domainkey.yourdomain.com), and the selector is chosen by whichever provider sends your mail -- there is no single fixed name to look up. This tool checks the selector names commonly used by Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Mailchimp/Mandrill, SendGrid, and a few generic defaults (google, selector1, selector2, k1, s1, s2, default, dkim, mail). If none of those resolve, that is not proof DKIM is missing -- check a sent message's own DKIM-Signature header, or your provider's dashboard, for the exact selector it uses.

Evidence, not a determination. This reads SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and BIMI DNS records and reports what they say -- it is not email deliverability, security, or DNS configuration advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional.

vs-checking-dns-records-by-hand.html.text:
← Email Authentication Checker

Email Authentication Checker vs. checking DNS records by hand with dig

Every developer and admin already has this move: run dig txt against a domain and read the record back. For a single top-level SPF or DMARC record, that is enough. This checker exists for the three things one dig call cannot show: the true recursive cost of an SPF include chain, which of many possible DKIM selector names your provider actually uses, and whether DMARC enforcement is strict enough for BIMI to display.

Where one dig call stops being enough

What you're trying to answerdig by handThis checker
What does my top-level SPF or DMARC record say?Works well. dig txt yourdomain.com and dig txt _dmarc.yourdomain.com show exactly this in one call each.Reads the same records, in the same run as the checks below.
Is my SPF record actually under RFC 7208's 10-DNS-lookup limit?Invisible to a single dig call -- each include:/redirect= mechanism can itself contain more of the same, and the limit counts the whole chain. Confirming it means recursively dig-ing every nested include and keeping a running total by hand.Follows every include:/redirect= mechanism recursively and sums the total against the 10-lookup budget automatically.
Which DKIM selector does my provider actually use?Not discoverable from DNS alone -- there is no fixed selector name, so you guess one, run dig txt <selector>._domainkey.yourdomain.com, and an NXDOMAIN only proves you guessed wrong, not that DKIM is missing.Checks nine common selector names used by major providers in one run and flags a revoked (empty p=) key if it finds one.
Will BIMI actually display in Gmail or Yahoo?Not answerable from the BIMI record alone -- it can look perfectly valid while staying invisible, because display also requires DMARC enforcement at p=quarantine/reject with pct=100. Answering this means reading two separate records and cross-checking them by hand.Reads the BIMI record and the DMARC policy together and reports whether enforcement is actually strong enough for BIMI to be honored.
Re-checking all of the above after a DNS or provider change.Several separate dig calls, recomputed and cross-referenced by hand, every time.One command, or one page load -- and the identical logic is a zero-dependency CLI you can gate CI on.

A single well-aimed dig txt call is still the fastest way to read a record you already know the name of, and this checker's own lookups are not doing anything dig couldn't -- they are the same kind of DNS queries, just walked recursively through every SPF include, tried against nine DKIM selector names, and cross-checked between BIMI and DMARC, instead of leaving that walking and cross-checking to be done, and remembered, by hand.

This tool needs no account: the browser page queries Cloudflare's public DNS-over-HTTPS resolver directly from your own browser, and the CLI does the same from your own machine. Neither ever sends the domain you check, or the records read, through this site.

Common questions

Can't I just run dig txt myself?

Yes, for the most obvious case: dig txt yourdomain.com will show your top-level SPF record, and dig txt _dmarc.yourdomain.com will show your DMARC policy. For that specific, most-obvious read, one command each is enough. The problem is the other three checks this tool does are not visible in any single dig response -- they only show up when you compare several DNS queries against each other, which is where running dig by hand stops being enough evidence.

How do I know which DKIM selector to check?

You don't, from DNS alone -- the selector is chosen by whichever provider sends your mail, and there is no single fixed name to dig for. By hand, that means guessing a selector, running dig txt selector._domainkey.yourdomain.com, getting NXDOMAIN, and trying another -- and NXDOMAIN on a guess you invented yourself proves nothing about whether DKIM is actually configured, only that you guessed a name nobody published a key at.

Why doesn't a clean top-level SPF record mean SPF actually passes?

Because RFC 7208 counts the whole recursive chain, not just your own record. A record with three include: mechanisms looks short in a single dig txt call, but each of those includes can itself contain further include:/redirect= mechanisms, and the 10-DNS-lookup budget is spent across the entire chain. Confirming you're under the limit means recursively dig-ing every nested include and keeping a running total by hand -- skip one level and you can be well over 10 while a single top-level read looks fine.

Can I tell from DNS alone whether BIMI will actually display?

Not from the BIMI record by itself. A dig txt default._bimi.yourdomain.com can return a perfectly valid-looking record while BIMI stays invisible in Gmail or Yahoo, because both require DMARC enforcement to be strict enough first -- p=quarantine or p=reject at pct=100. Answering "will this display" means reading the BIMI record and the DMARC record separately and cross-checking one against the other, not reading either alone.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes a manual method every developer and admin already has -- running dig (or nslookup, or a browser-based DNS lookup tool) and reading the TXT records by eye. It names no competing product or company. The checker's own browser page and CLI query Cloudflare's public DNS-over-HTTPS resolver directly, never through this site.

Email Authentication Checker vs. MXToolbox

Two different shapes: MXToolbox is a broad network- and mail-diagnostic platform — MX records, blacklist status, SMTP diagnostics, and SPF/DKIM/DMARC among many other tools — with ongoing monitoring and alerting sold as an account-based product. This page is a free, no-account checker focused specifically on SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and BIMI, with a recursive RFC 7208 SPF lookup count and a matching CI-gateable CLI.

What each tool is for

MXToolbox is a network- and mail-diagnostic platform used by network and mail administrators, covering MX record lookups, blacklist status across many block-list providers, SMTP banner and connectivity diagnostics, and SPF/DKIM/DMARC lookups among a large catalog of other tools. Its ongoing monitoring, alerting, and blacklist-watch features are sold through an account-based product. MXToolbox's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names, monitoring limits, or pricing, so only its well-documented category and identity are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This checker does one narrower thing in more depth. It recursively walks every include:/redirect= mechanism in your SPF record and sums the total against RFC 7208's 10-DNS-lookup limit across the whole chain, not just the top-level record — the single most common real-world SPF bug. It checks DKIM at nine common selector names and flags a revoked (empty p=) key, reads DMARC's policy, pct=, reporting addresses, and alignment mode, and checks whether BIMI is honored by DMARC enforcement. Every finding names the exact record and tag it read, not a bare pass/fail score. It runs free in any browser, and the identical logic ships as a zero-dependency Node CLI you can run as a CI gate against your own domain. No account, no monitoring dashboard, nothing stored beyond an anonymous local counter.

I want the same SPF/DKIM/DMARC/BIMI check to run automatically before every deploy, as a CI gate.This checker's zero-dependency CLI (cli.mjs), run against your own domain.
I need blacklist monitoring, SMTP connectivity diagnostics, or ongoing alerting across many mail/network signals.MXToolbox, or a comparable platform — this checker has none of those features.
Do I need an account to use the tool?This checker: no. MXToolbox's monitoring and alerting features are sold through an account-based product.
Is anything I check ever uploaded or stored on a server?This checker: no — the browser page and the CLI both query Cloudflare's public DNS resolver directly, never through this site.

Someone who wants a single broad diagnostic dashboard with ongoing monitoring and alerting across many mail and network signals is better served by MXToolbox or a comparable platform.
